title: 3 reasons why you shouldn't buy the Rogue Matador dip bar
summary: A critical review of the Rogue Matador rack dip attachment. The handles are an awkward diameter (he fixes this with fat grips), the angled arms internally rotate his shoulders, and it shakes even on a rack bolted into concrete. It's fine for occasional dippers but bad for calisthenics enthusiasts and for weighted dips.

claims.claim: The Rogue Matador attaches to the rack with a pin through the side and back holes, and because of its size it only fits on the wide side of the rack.
The Matador handles are an awkward diameter: too big to wrap comfortably (it strains the wrist), too small for a stable thumbless grip.
Putting fat grips on the dip handles makes them wide enough to use thumbless or wrapped and just rest your hands on.
For his build, parallel dip bars are most comfortable; the Matador's angled arms internally rotate his shoulders, which feels bad and hurts if he goes deep.
His shoulders can't take Gironda-style dips; on the Matador he has to use a Slingshot to deload the bottom of the dip.
The Matador shakes even on a rack bolted deep into concrete, more so as you rep; at 210 lb it's not dangerous for him, but it could be for heavier lifters.
The Matador's welding is good quality and the pin fits well, but the paint chips by itself; price is reasonable at about 80-100 dollars.
Buy the Matador only if you dip occasionally and have mastered dips; calisthenics enthusiasts and anyone doing weighted dips should avoid it or risk destroying their shoulders.
The Matador is one of the few Rogue products he doesn't like or recommend.
